hints: Think where the nitro group can go relative to the methyl group when methyl is 2,4-directing, given the para product is already shown.
walkthrough:
Use the directing effect of methyl**
Picture methylbenzene. The $\text{CH}_3$ group pushes electron density into the ring and directs the incoming electrophile to the 2,4 and 6 positions. The product shown has $\text{NO}_2$ para to $\text{CH}_3$, so the other allowed position is ortho to $\text{CH}_3$.
Final answer: 2-nitromethylbenzene: benzene ring with $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{NO}_2$ in ortho (1,2) positions.

hints: Recall which strong electrophile attacks the benzene ring in nitration and which two acids combine to make it.
walkthrough:
Build the nitronium ion**
Sulfuric acid acts as a strong acid toward nitric acid. Two molecules of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ protonate $\text{HNO}_3$, which then loses water as $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$. What is left is the powerful electrophile $\text{NO}_2^+$, with $2\text{HSO}_4^-$ as counter ions. Balance H, N, O, S and charge to get the equation above.
Final answer: $\text{HNO}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NO}_2^+ + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + 2\text{HSO}_4^-$

hints: Compare the pi system in methylbenzene, where all six p orbitals overlap, with intermediate T where one carbon now has four single bonds.
Count how many pi electrons remain delocalised in T versus the six in methylbenzene.
Think what hybridisation and bond angle that tetrahedral saturated carbon in T must have compared with the planar $sp^2$ carbons in methylbenzene.
walkthrough:
See what the electrophile does to the ring**
In methylbenzene the six p orbitals overlap side on to give a continuous ring of delocalised pi electrons above and below the plane. When $\text{NO}_2^+$ bonds to one carbon in T, that carbon forms two new sigma bonds to H and to $\text{NO}_2$ and can no longer contribute a p orbital.

Count the remaining pi electrons**
Methylbenzene has six delocalised pi electrons. In T only five carbons are still $sp^2$, so only four pi electrons remain in the delocalised system. The aromatic sextet is lost, which is why T is high energy.

Spot the $sp^3$ centre**
All carbons in methylbenzene are $sp^2$ with $120^\circ$ bond angles and equal C-C bond lengths. In T the attacked carbon becomes $sp^3$ hybridised, tetrahedral with bond angles near $109.5^\circ$. So C-C bonds in T are no longer all the same length and not all angles are $120^\circ$.

Final answer: In T delocalisation is disrupted, pi bonding extends over only five carbons, not six.
T has only four pi electrons delocalised, methylbenzene has six.
One carbon in T is $sp^3$ hybridised (tetrahedral, $109.5^\circ$), all carbons in methylbenzene are $sp^2$ planar ($120^\circ$); so bond lengths and angles in T are not all equal.

hints: Look at compound W with $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{NH}_2$ para to each other and name it as a substituted benzoic acid.
walkthrough:
Name from the acid end**
The $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group makes the parent benzoic acid, with carbon 1 at the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. The $\text{NH}_2$ group is opposite it, in the para or 4 position. So the systematic name is 4-aminobenzoic acid.

hints: Start with step 1, reduction of $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$, and recall the classic Sn and concentrated HCl system.
For step 2, forming $\text{NHCOCH}_3$ from $\text{NH}_2$, think which acyl chloride acetylates amines.
For step 3, oxidising $\text{CH}_3$ to $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ while the amine is protected, recall hot alkaline or acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$.
For step 4, think how an amide $\text{NHCOCH}_3$ is hydrolysed back to $\text{NH}_2$ using aqueous acid and heat.
For step 5, forming the ethyl ester $\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ from $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, recall the alcohol plus concentrated sulfuric acid method.
Check why protection was needed: hot $\text{KMnO}_4$ would otherwise oxidise the free $\text{NH}_2$ group.
walkthrough:
Reduce the nitro group**
Step 1 converts $\text{Ar-NO}_2$ to $\text{Ar-NH}_2$. Use tin with concentrated hydrochloric acid, heated under reflux, followed by neutralisation to release the free amine. This is the standard Paper 4 reduction.

Protect the amine**
The free $\text{NH}_2$ would be oxidised in step 3, so protect it as $\text{NHCOCH}_3$ using ethanoyl chloride, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$. The amine attacks the carbonyl carbon and HCl is lost.

Oxidise the methyl side chain**
Now oxidise $\text{Ar-CH}_3$ to $\text{Ar-CO}_2\text{H}$ with hot acidified or alkaline potassium manganate(VII), $\text{KMnO}_4$. The protected amide survives these conditions.

Deprotect back to the amine**
Hydrolyse the amide $\text{Ar-NHCOCH}_3$ back to $\text{Ar-NH}_2$ (compound W) using aqueous $\text{HCl}$ with heat. This gives ethanoic acid as the co-product.

Make the ethyl ester**
Finally esterify $\text{Ar-CO}_2\text{H}$ to $\text{Ar-CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (benzocaine) with ethanol in the presence of concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heated under reflux.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{Sn}$ + conc. $\text{HCl}$, heat / reflux (reduction $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$)
step 2: $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ (formation of amide)
step 3: acidified or alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ / $\text{MnO}_4^-$, heat (oxidation $\text{CH}_3$ to $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$)
step 4: aq. $\text{HCl}$, heat (acid hydrolysis of amide to amine)
step 5: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ + conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heat / reflux (esterification)

hints: Compare the nitrogen lone pair in benzocaine, attached directly to a benzene ring, with that in ethylamine, attached to an alkyl group.
Think how delocalisation into the ring versus electron donation from an ethyl group changes how readily the lone pair accepts $\text{H}^+$.
walkthrough:
Link basicity to the lone pair**
Basicity means willingness to accept a proton, $\text{H}^+$, using the lone pair on nitrogen. The more available that lone pair, the stronger the base.

Contrast aromatic and aliphatic amines**
In benzocaine the nitrogen is directly bonded to the benzene ring, so its lone pair overlaps with the ring pi system and is delocalised over the ring. It is pulled away and less free to bond to $\text{H}^+$. In ethylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, the ethyl group pushes electron density toward nitrogen by the inductive effect, making the lone pair more available. So ethylamine is the stronger base.

Final answer: Benzocaine is less basic than ethylamine as its N lone pair is less available to accept $\text{H}^+$.
In benzocaine the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring (phenyl is electron withdrawing), whereas in ethylamine the ethyl group is electron donating, increasing lone pair availability.

hints: Count unique carbon environments in para-disubstituted benzocaine, remembering the ring has a plane of symmetry.
walkthrough:
Count symmetry-unique carbons**
Benzocaine is $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ para substituted. The benzene ring gives 4 distinct environments (C-N, C-C=O, and two pairs of equivalent CH carbons). Add $\text{C=O}$, $\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3$ to get $4 + 3 = 7$ peaks in the $^{13}$C NMR spectrum.
Final answer: 7 peaks

hints: Think what $^1$H NMR detects and whether $\text{CDCl}_3$ contains any $^1$H to give a signal compared with $\text{CHCl}_3$.
walkthrough:
Keep the solvent invisible**
Proton NMR detects $^1$H nuclei only. $\text{CHCl}_3$ has one proton that would absorb and swamp the spectrum. Replacing H by D to give $\text{CDCl}_3$ removes that $^1$H signal because deuterium resonates at a very different frequency.
Final answer: $\text{CDCl}_3$ contains no $^1$H / deuterium is not detected in proton NMR, so gives no signal, whereas $\text{CHCl}_3$ would give a peak.

hints: Assign the $\delta$ 1.2 triplet to the $\text{CH}_3$ next to $\text{CH}_2$ using the Data Booklet alkyl region.
Assign the $\delta$ 3.5 quartet to the $\text{O-CH}_2$ deshielded by oxygen and split by three neighbours.
Assign the $\delta$ 5.5 singlet to $\text{NH}_2$ with no adjacent protons to split it.
Assign the $\delta$ 7.1 to 7.4 multiplet to the four aromatic protons on the para-disubstituted ring.
walkthrough:
Read the ethyl group**
At $\delta$ 1.2 the three $\text{CH}_3$ protons next to $\text{CH}_2$ appear as a triplet. At $\delta$ 3.5 the two $\text{O-CH}_2$ protons are more deshielded by the electronegative oxygen and appear as a quartet. Triplet plus quartet is the classic ethyl pattern.

Pick out the amine protons**
At $\delta$ 5.5 the two $\text{NH}_2$ protons have no protons on the adjacent nitrogen-bearing carbon to couple with, so they give a broad singlet. N-H protons often exchange and appear broad.

Assign the aromatic protons**
At $\delta$ 7.1 to 7.4 the four protons on the para-disubstituted benzene ring are strongly deshielded and couple with each other in a complex way, giving a multiplet integrating to 4H.

Final answer: $\delta$ 1.2: $\text{CH}_3$, 3H, triplet; $\delta$ 3.5: $\text{CH}_2\text{O}$, 2H, quartet; $\delta$ 5.5: $\text{NH}_2$, 2H, singlet (broad); $\delta$ 7.1-7.4: aromatic / benzene H, 4H, multiplet.

hints: Apply the n+1 rule to the $\delta$ 1.2 $\text{CH}_3$ signal and count protons on the neighbouring carbon.
walkthrough:
Apply n+1**
The $\delta$ 1.2 peak is the $\text{CH}_3$ of $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH}_2\text{-O}$. The neighbouring carbon carries two equivalent protons, so $n = 2$ and $n+1 = 3$ lines, a triplet.
Final answer: Triplet because adjacent / neighbouring carbon ($\text{CH}_2\text{O}$) has two protons, $n+1 = 3$.

hints: Think which protons in benzocaine are labile N-H protons that can exchange with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ and disappear from proton NMR.
walkthrough:
Spot the exchangeable protons**
N-H protons are labile and rapidly swap with D from $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ to give N-D. Deuterium does not show in the proton spectrum, so the $\delta$ 5.5 $\text{NH}_2$ singlet vanishes.
Final answer: Peak at $\delta$ 5.5 ($\text{NH}_2$) disappears as $\text{NH}_2$ protons exchange with deuterium from $\text{D}_2\text{O}$.

hints: Recall the low temperature reagents that convert a primary aromatic amine to a diazonium salt.
walkthrough:
Form nitrous acid in situ**
Diazotisation of the primary aromatic amine in benzocaine needs nitrous acid, $\text{HNO}_2$, made fresh from sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid and kept cold below $10^\circ\text{C}$ to stabilise the diazonium salt R.
Final answer: $\text{NaNO}_2$ + $\text{HCl}$ (forming $\text{HNO}_2$), below $10^\circ\text{C}$.

hints: Draw R as the para-ester benzene diazonium ion, $\text{EtO}_2\text{C-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N}_2^+$.
Draw S as the azo compound formed by coupling R para to the OH of phenol, linked by $\text{-N=N-}$.
walkthrough:
Draw the diazonium salt R**
Keep the ethyl ester group para to nitrogen. Diazotisation turns $\text{-NH}_2$ into $\text{-N}^+\equiv\text{N}$, so R is $p\text{-CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}_2\text{C-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N}_2^+$.

Couple to form the azo dye S**
In alkaline solution phenol couples with the diazonium ion para to the $\text{OH}$ group. Join the two rings with an $\text{-N=N-}$ bridge to give $p\text{-CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}_2\text{C-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N=N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-OH}$ (para,para). This extended conjugated system is the coloured dyestuff S.

Final answer: R: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}_2\text{C-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N}^+\equiv\text{N}$ (para diazonium ion derived from benzocaine).
S: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}_2\text{C-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N=N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-OH}$ (para to para azo dye with phenol).
